chapter_theme: Civakan and his company cross the five landscapes in turn, the desert in a single day, reach Videham and send word to its king, who orders a welcome; the city throngs to see him, hails him with the names of Kama and Murugan, and its women plead with his elephants to walk slowly.

cast.role: the hero, travelling to Videham and welcomed into its city
the young men of Civakan's company (திறலார், தீதிலார், இளையவர்)
the king of Videham (விதையம்), who orders the welcome; not named in these verses
the king's people of Videham, who meet the guest with gifts
the crowds of the city of Videham, who gather and hail Civakan (நகரம், ஏனையவர்)
the women of the towns and city of Videham, who praise, gaze at and bless Civakan
the elephants of Civakan's entry, the she-elephant (இரும்பிடி) and the tusker (சிறுபிடி கேள்வன்) the women address

2102.reading: Civakan's company, strong as lions, passes through the marutam fields, where a buffalo with udders like pots grazes the kuvalai and its sweet milk, spilled wherever it walks, feeds the young of swans, herons and storks, and their great bells ring as they go.
2102.nuance: The verse opens a journey through all five landscapes in order: marutam (2102), neytal (2103), mullai (2104), kurinji (2105) and palai (2106-2107).
2102.event: Civakan and his company pass through the farm country of the marutam fields.

2103.reading: Watching a swan that, among the conches circling a right-whorled conch on the shore, embraces one as its mate and then reels in distress to find it is not, the faultless travellers leave the neytal shore on their right.
2103.nuance: The swan's mistake of a conch for its mate is a small figure of desire deceived by likeness, set in the landscape the travellers merely pass.
2103.event: The company passes the seashore of the neytal country.

2104.reading: Where the buck and doe sleep under the konrai and bees drink the flowers as good men drink the smiling faces of the country's young women, the mullai forest comes out to meet them with its fragrance as they walk.
2104.event: The company walks through the mullai forest.

2105.reading: They cross the kurinji, where on the bamboo hill a tusker stands and plays with a stream falling on its tusks, like the lord of the bright trident who takes cold water on his spread matted hair with the young white moon, and where peacocks gather like women in their grace.
2105.nuance: The elephant under the waterfall is likened to the trident-bearer receiving the river on his matted hair with the crescent, Siva's image used as ornament in a Jain epic, with no claim about the god.
2105.event: The company crosses the hill country.

2106.reading: At sunset they mount their leaping horses for the hard desert track, hot as if one trod on fire, where red-combed jungle fowl call among the kadamba with the hooked-beaked kites, their bodies covered with sandal like moonbeams.
2106.nuance: They take the desert by night and against the heat cover themselves with sandal paste.
2106.event: At nightfall the company rides into the palai desert.

2107.reading: Not stopping, they cross the burning desert within a single day, as quickly as the wealth of one who seeks the generous fame that stands in an unstable world goes from him, as desire goes from the hearts of the learned when a young woman's messenger comes, and as the anger of the holy passes.
2107.nuance: The three similes are three things that do not stay, and each is praise: the fame-seeker's wealth leaves because he gives it away, the learned man's desire leaves because he masters it, the anger of the holy leaves because it is brief. கடவுளர் may mean gods or the holy ascetics; the second simile's line (தூதின் ... கலைவலார் நெஞ்சிற் காமம்) is compressed and its sense is my best construal.
2107.event: The company crosses the desert in one day.

claims.claim: in an unstable world it is generous fame that stands, and the wealth of one who seeks it does not stay
the anger of holy men does not last

2108.reading: On the bank of this river, ringed by cool water where bakula trees shed flowers as if honey dripped from them and the hum of herons and bees meets the stream, the young men breathe out their weariness and rise.
2108.event: The young men rest on a river bank after the desert and set out again.

2109.reading: Reaching the water-rich groves of Videham, where the spotted crab carries fallen jackfruit and banana to ease the craving of its pregnant mate, they send men ahead to tell the king.
2109.nuance: The crab feeding its pregnant mate is the last of the journey's small domestic scenes before the human welcome begins. The third line, on the snail and the turtle, is hard to construe.
2109.event: The company reaches Videham and sends word ahead to its king.

2110.reading: The king writes his order on the palm-leaf in the royal hand, that his people in every house should stand close together like the fingers in a bow-guard and receive the guest as one, and they heap up the nectars of the land, the sea, the hills and the forest and go out to meet him on the wide outskirts.
2110.nuance: The four nectars (land, sea, hill, forest) gather the landscapes the company has just crossed into the welcome itself.
2110.event: The king of Videham orders his people by written decree to receive Civakan, and they meet him with the produce of all four lands.

2111.reading: Women with gold-laden breasts open their red mouths in praise, strew flowers and bow, plant fruiting areca and plantain, and carry fragrant smoke like a mountain's mist, so that every town is like the world of the gods.
2111.event: The women of the towns line the road, praising and worshipping the guest.

2112.reading: The gates and temples, the halls, theatres and avenues of the mansioned city, like a great mountain loud with falls, all gather to see the noble one.
2112.event: The whole city gathers to see Civakan.

2113.reading: On one side the bright golden bands tied on the brows of beautiful women, decked with many-rayed necklaces and ornaments, their young breasts fierce as tusks, shine.

2114.reading: On one side is the beauty of the women who come out in throngs to see the lord, scattering powder and wreaths, their long hair and the anklets on their feet sounding as they rise.
2114.event: The women run out in crowds to see Civakan.

2115.reading: On one side the bright women, whose grace mocks the flowering creeper, run on each other's heels, pearls heaving on their young breasts and their tinkling anklet bells ringing.

2116.reading: On one side the well-jewelled women who have crowded the cloud-touching mansions, breasts bound tight in bodices and waists sagging, let their large eyes roam.

2117.reading: On one side, women with flashing earrings and garlands fill the golden mansions until they are hidden, gathered like a flock of spotted peacocks, rich in their fixed array.

2118.reading: On one side the singing women and the dancing women with many-stranded girdles run through every market street, and the ornaments that fall and break from them split the long darkness with their light.
2118.nuance: The printed line division cuts words across lines (அல்கு/ல், தொ/றோட); read across, the sense is clear.

2119.reading: With women of curved earrings and men alike crowding the street and the terraces above to see, garlands tangle with garlands and the pollen of the flowers makes every place like a spread carpet.
2119.event: Men and women crowd the street and the roofs.

2120.reading: Seeing the lord on the elephant's neck, like the young war god, in the midst of a sea of army while yak-tail whisks drive the bees from him, the others too rejoice and cry out.
2120.nuance: அமா குமரனின் is probably for அமர் குமரனின், Kumaran of battle, that is Murugan.
2120.event: Civakan rides into the city on an elephant amid his army, and the crowd raises a cry.

2121.reading: Let fortune enter, with lovely eyes of honeyed flowers; let the bridegroom of the great flower garland enter; let Kama enter, let the bull among men enter; let the famed and handsome Nambi of the Vidyadharas enter.
2121.nuance: Each title recalls something told earlier: the bridegroom of the marriages, the Kama the women took him for, the one bound to the Vidyadharas through Gandharvadattai's marriage. திருவே may hail him as fortune itself or as the one who has fortune.
2121.event: The crowd hails Civakan as he enters, giving him one title after another.

2122.reading: Let the one of the spear who slew the lightning-touching mountain enter; let the Yaksha of the sweet-honeyed garland enter; let the victor enter, let the hero enter: so the city came out to meet him.
2122.nuance: The spear-bearer who slew the mountain is Murugan who split the Krauncha; the Yaksha likely recalls Sudanjanan, the yaksha god who befriended him. The acclaim gives Civakan the god's names without the epic claiming he is the god.
2122.event: The city welcomes Civakan with acclaim.

2123.reading: Scattering fragrant pounded powder on every side and showering scented garlands and wreaths, women with waists that shame the drum, red mouths like the tondai fruit and eyes that shame the blade stand blessing him.
2123.nuance: துடியடு and வடியடு are best read with அடு, 'to defeat' (a waist that outdoes the drum's narrow middle, eyes that outdo the blade), not as lost -யொடு.
2123.event: The women shower Civakan with powder and garlands and bless him.

2124.reading: Holding out bee-swarmed garlands in worship, the women say: great she-elephant, we learned our gait from you; if you love us, walk slowly, so that we may see Kama with our dark eyes.
2124.nuance: The conventional figure that women walk like a she-elephant becomes a claim of kinship on the beast: having taught us our gait, she owes us a slow one.
2124.event: The women beg the elephant carrying Civakan to walk slowly so they can look at him longer.

2125.reading: Others sulk, their ornaments shifting and breasts heaving: you have not understood that a gentle gait is the beauty of womanhood; you have learned a rough gait; you will lose your husband; you are no she-elephant, you wretch.
2125.nuance: The rule of womanly gait is put playfully in the mouths of women who are themselves running in the streets after a stranger; the epic neither endorses nor answers it here.
2125.event: Some of the women scold the elephant for carrying Civakan past too fast.

claims.claim: a gentle gait is the beauty of womanhood, and a woman who walks roughly will lose her husband

2126.reading: And others say to the tusker, husband of the small she-elephant with hairy mouth, small eyes, large ears and great feet, who vies with Airavata: carry the lord who guards our lives and stand and help us.
2126.nuance: The address turns from the she-elephant of 2124-2125 to her mate; which beast Civakan rides the verses leave unclear. The last line (உயிர்கா வலற்கொண் டுதவநில்) is hard to construe: 'the guardian of life' may be Civakan, guardian of their lives, or the elephant asked to guard his.
2126.event: Women ask the tusker to halt with Civakan.

links.note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; 2107 takes the same unstable world and fame that stands, and uses the fame-seeker's wealth as a figure of what vanishes fast.
links.teaches: The pair shows the price side of the Kural's maxim: the fame that alone stands is bought with wealth that goes as fast as a desert crossed in a day, so lasting renown and fleeting riches are one transaction.

gains.a: the simile's ground, why a fame-seeker's wealth should be the very type of the fleeting, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: a concrete measure of how quickly the giver's wealth leaves him, which the couplet's praise of fame never shows

links.note: Kural 29 speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of virtue, held even for a moment; 2107 counts the anger of the holy among things that do not stay.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's crux over whether such anger lasts only a moment or is unbearable for a moment is settled one way in the epic, which takes its brevity as proverbial enough to serve as a simile of speed.

gains.a: a source and authority for the figure of the holy man's short-lived anger, which the epic uses without explaining
gains.b: an early reader's construal of its disputed second line, showing the brevity reading in use as common speech

links.note: The women of another city asked whether Civakan was the Vel of the kadamba or the son of the five arrows; Videham's crowd hails him as both, the spear-bearer who slew the mountain and Kama.
links.teaches: What was a puzzled question of desire in one city becomes a public litany of titles in the next, so the likeness to Murugan and Kama hardens from a woman's doubt into the name a whole city gives him.

links.note: In 2124 the women claim they learned their gait from the she-elephant and plead for a slow walk; in 2125 others call the same beast no she-elephant for its rough gait.
links.teaches: The two verses turn one convention, woman's gait as a she-elephant's, against itself: the beast that is the model of womanly walking is scolded for failing womanhood when its speed takes the hero from their sight.

source_issues: 2102-2111 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2123 lines 3-4 are flagged for a possible lost vowel sign (துடியடு, வடியடு); both read well as அடு 'defeat' and are best left unrepaired.
2120 line 2 அமா குமரனின் is probably a corruption of அமர் குமரனின்.
2118 lines 1-3 are divided across words (அல்கு/ல், தொ/றோட) by the printed line breaks.
2126 line 4 (உயிர்கா வலற்கொண் டுதவநில்) is hard to construe; 2109 line 3 and 2106 line 4 are also obscure.
